segments.text: Let's turn today to Acts of the Apostles chapter 12 and verse 1.
Now about that time, Herod the king laid hands on some who belonged to the church in order to mistreat them.
And he had James the brother of John put to death with a sword.
And when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also.
Now this was during the days of the Feast of Unleavened Bread.
There's one thing we see here about Herod that when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he arrested Peter also.
Here was a king who decided his policies depending on what pleased the people.
And you find towards the end of the chapter how God punishes him by killing him for taking the glory to himself.
Here was a man who had been refused by Jesus to even converse with him.
And to whom Jesus did not speak a word or show a miracle or any such thing because his heart had already been hardened through slaying John the Baptist, going against his conscience.
There he sought to please the people. Here we find he seeks to please the people.
But God is sovereign. God could have saved James from death, just like as we see later on in Acts 12, how he saved Peter from death.
We read of an angel coming in to deliver Peter. That same angel could have come a few days earlier and delivered James as well.
Why didn't God do that? Our human mind cannot understand the way God works.
God's working is very different from our human understanding. God's ways are not our ways.
He alone knows when the time for a particular person's life and ministry on earth is over.
And it is clear that James' time on earth was over. Nobody could have killed James if his time was not yet over.

God was sovereign. So we need to see this contrast between James and Peter because we face similar situations today as to why God allows certain believers to suffer in a particular way and certain other believers seem to go freely, certain die very young and certain live to an older age.
It's got nothing to do with one being wholehearted or not. If both could be wholehearted, it's got to do with God's plan for their lives and for each of our lives God's plan is different.
And so we see here verse 4, when Herodot sees Peter, he put him in prison, delivering him to four squads of soldiers to guard him.
In other words, 16 soldiers were there to guard one man, intending after the Passover to bring him out before the people.
So Peter was kept in the prison, but prayer for him was being made fervently by the Church of God.
The Church did not comprise in those days of influential people, which is a good thing, otherwise they would have depended on man.
But they did have influence in heaven far more than today, where the Church has more influential people on earth and not so much influence in heaven.
Because they don't have faith, because maybe their lives are not right. But in those days, the Church, their lives were right.
They walked in a clear conscience, they had faith, and they believed God could do anything.
And they prayed fervently. And what was the result? God answered immediately.
It says here in verse 6, on the very night when Herod was about to bring him forward, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers,
bound with two chains, one hand bound to each soldier, and guards in front of the door were watching over the prison.
And an angel of the Lord suddenly appeared, and a light shone in the cell, and he struck Peter's side, roused him, saying,
Get up quickly. And his chains fell off his hands, and the angel said to him, Guard yourself, put on your sandals.
And he did so, and he said to him, Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.
And he went out and continued to follow, and he did not know what was being done, but the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision.
And when they had passed the first and second guard, they came to the iron gate that leads into the city, which opened for them by itself.
And they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel departed from him.
And when Peter came to himself, he said, Now I know for sure that the Lord has sent forth his angel, and rescued me from the hand of Herod,
from all that the Jewish people were expecting.
Now, a number of things, significant things that we can learn from this passage.
First of all, that when we pray fervently, God hears.
He doesn't always answer in the same way. Perhaps prayer was also made when James was in prison.
But God did not choose to answer the prayer the way the church expected it at that time.
So God's answers are not always according to what we think is best.
But we can certainly believe that God hears and answers prayer. There's no doubt about that.
The other thing we see here is that even though Peter knew that perhaps the fate of James awaited him also in a day or so,
it says here that he was sleeping. Verse 6, it's wonderful to be so much at rest in God,
so that even if you know you're going to be killed tomorrow morning, you can have a sound sleep tonight,
because your life is in God's hands. It's wonderful to see that Peter was sleeping.
He wasn't restless. He committed his cause to God, his conscience was clear, and he had no fear.
And so he was sleeping. And then we see how the angel of the Lord appeared and opened up the cell and his chains fell off.
A beautiful picture of salvation as well. When Christ comes and delivers us from the prison of sin, this is how it is.
However many chains of lust and however many demons and sins we may have been enslaved to in the past, the chains fall off.
The light shines in and we walk forth free. That's how the Lord sets us free.
And Peter was sure finally, he first thought it was a vision, but he finally knew this is the hand of the Lord that rescued me from the hand of Herod.
And what did he do? Verse 12, when he realized this, he went to the house of Mary.
That's interesting. We don't know where Peter's home was, but he moved immediately to the fellowship of the church.
We see that earlier in chapter 5 also, that when they were released from prison, they went to their own.
Their fellowship with the brothers and sisters in the church was so deep that the first thought that occurred to them when they were delivered, oh God answered prayer in a supernatural way.
Was to go straight to the fellowship of the church and to go to house of Mary, the mother of John, who was also called Mark.
And there in the middle of the night, many people were praying. Just think how earnestly they were praying for Peter's deliverance.
And when he knocked at the door of the gate, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer and when she recognized Peter's voice, because of her joy, she did not open the gate.
But ran in and announced that Peter was standing in front of the gate. And they said to her, you're out of your mind.
But she kept insisting that it was so and they kept saying it's his angel. They thought he had died.
And there's something interesting that we can see there also, that even though they didn't have so much faith, yet God answered.
Faith as a mustard seed was enough. Their faith was manifested in the fact that they prayed.
But they never expected the answer to come while they were praying.
In Isaiah, God says, while they are calling, I will hear and before they call, I will answer.

And they didn't expect the answer to come so quickly. Their faith was not so strong, so that when Rhoda came and said, Peter has come to the gate, they should have jumped up and said, well, praise the Lord, God has answered our prayer.
But that's not what they said. They said, no, that can't be.
They'd just been praying that Peter would be released, but when he came to the gate, they wouldn't believe it.
Well, that's an encouragement to us to know that our faith doesn't have to be perfect, completely free from all element of doubt.
Before God answers, God is merciful. The very fact that we pray and we trust and we keep on praying proves that we trust in God.
And finally, when they went there, they saw it was Peter, indeed, and they were amazed.
But Peter, verse 17, motioned to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had let him out of the prison.
And he said, report these things to James. Now James is, there was the brother of Jesus who was converted after the resurrection.
And he was now the leader in the church in Jerusalem. So he said, report these things to James and the brethren.
And he departed from there and went to another place. There's something we can see there too, that when the Lord does something spectacular for us,
there can be a great lust in us to go around giving our testimony in every single place.
Now it's enough that we briefly tell people who are praying for us what God has done, but not to go around testifying in such a way as to draw attention to ourselves.
Peter never stayed on there. He just went on to another place. He'd been called to preach the gospel, not to keep on giving his testimony how he was delivered from prison.
In fact, when you read Peter's letters, one Peter and two Peter, you never find him referring to the time when he was released from prison or when he raised Tabitha from the dead or any such thing.
No, his letters are full of exhortations to a holy life. He doesn't emphasize testimony about the miracles he has seen.
So different from the testimonies we hear today. He departed and went to another place. And when the day came, there was no small disturbance among the soldiers as to what could have become of Peter.
And when Herod had searched for him and had not found him, he examined the guards and ordered that they be led away to execution.
And he went down from Judea to Caesarean to spending his time there. Herod was really surprised that Peter wasn't found.
And yet his hard heart would not be convicted. His hard heart was not convicted when John the Baptist was killed.

By him, his hard heart was not convicted when Jesus stood before him. And even here, when Peter escaped supernaturally, he doesn't even consider the possibility that a God Almighty has done a miracle.
When a man goes down the way of a bad conscience, his heart gets hotter and hotter and hotter, and it is impossible for God to speak to him.
And in the following portion of the same chapter, we find out God punishes him finally with death.
We can learn many lessons from this chapter, warnings and encouragement.

Let's turn today to Acts of the Apostles, chapter 12 and verse 20. Here we read about Herod, who had just killed James the Apostle and had tried to kill Peter, but the Lord had delivered Peter from prison, as we considered in our last study.
And Herod, hardened in heart, goes down to Caesarea. We read in verse 20 that Herod was very angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and with one accord they came to him.
And having won over Blasters, the king's chamberlain, they were asking for peace, because their country was fed by the king's country.
And on an appointed day Herod, having put on his royal apparel, took his seat on the rostrum and began delivering an address to them.
And the people kept crying out the voice of a God and not of a man.
And immediately an angel of the Lord struck him because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and died.
This was the last chance that God gave Herod. God had been very long suffering with Herod through the years.
He had killed John the Baptist, he had ignored the claims of Jesus when Jesus stood before him, he had killed James, he tried to kill Peter.
And even after Peter was released from prison, he would not try to hear what God was trying to say to him.
And now, when he took the glory to himself, when people said, this is the voice of a God and not a man, he did not give God the glory.
He was eaten by worms and died. What a message there is here for those of us who preach God's word.
Particularly if you are gifted in preaching God's word.
There can be so many people in the audience who are gripped by what we speak and who are challenged and encouraged and comforted and helped.
And who can come to us and say words that are very similar to what's written here in verse 22.
You're really the mouthpiece of God. This is not an ordinary man, you're a prophet, etc. The voice of a God and not of a man.
And it says here immediately, verse 23, the angel of the Lord did not give Herod 24 hours to think about it.
He should have given God the glory immediately. As soon as people praise us, we must recognize what do we have that we have not received, like we read in 1 Corinthians 4.
What have you got that you did not receive? 1 Corinthians 4-7.
Nothing. Everything was received. Think of the incident where the disciples distributed the five loaves and two fish that Jesus multiplied to thousands of people who were scattered over the hillside.
And some people in the far periphery of the crowd may not have seen how this miracle took place.
And when a disciple brought the basket of the loaves and the fish and they ate it and they were amazed at the quantity that was available, they could have thanked the disciple.
And if the disciple took the credit to himself and gave them the impression that he was the one who had created or multiplied those loaves and fish, what a terrible sin that would have been.
He would have had to say immediately, no, it was not I who produced this, it was Jesus, I'm only distributing it.
We can recognize it in that situation, but it's exactly the same when we preach God's word.
If what we preach is really anointed, then we have to admit that God gave it to us.
Of course, there's a lot of preaching that comes from the human brain, and that's worthless for God's kingdom.

But that which comes from God, which we speak, which he speaks through our mouth and puts into our mind, if we take the credit for it, in fact, if we take the credit for anything, what have you got that you did not receive?
Even your brain and your health and your ability to speak is given by God.
God told Moses in Exodus chapter four, who is the one who makes people to speak and makes people dumb? Is it not I, the Lord?
Who is the one who has given us the ability to speak? It's the Lord.
So we must give God the glory immediately. This is a tremendous warning.
This is the spirit of the antichrist to sit in the church as though you're God, that when people give you the glory that should be given to God, you take it.
And when you take it, God takes note of it. And if not physical death, spiritual death enters in. You get eaten by worms in your soul, if not any other way, in any other place.
But in contrast, we read in verse 24, the word of the Lord continued to grow and to be multiplied. There is a but there.
Here are people like Herod who seek glory for themselves and try to hinder God's work, but it doesn't succeed.
But the word of the Lord continued to grow and to be multiplied.
And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had fulfilled their mission, taking along with them John, who was also called Mark.
No doubt, Barnabas and Saul had been in that prayer meeting where they had seen the tremendous power of prayer when they were praying for Peter's release, as we read in verse 12 of chapter 12.
And also earlier in verse 5 of chapter 12.
Barnabas and Saul, we read in chapter 11 verse 30, had brought a contribution of money for the poor saints in Judea.

Each of them determined to send a contribution. We read in chapter 11 verse 29. What a wonderful spirit those believers in Antioch had.
Each one of them, without exception, decided to give something to help the poor saints in Jerusalem who are going to face a famine as prophesied by Agabus.
Barnabas and Saul were selected to take this money and they came to Jerusalem. And when they came to Jerusalem, that was the time when Peter was in prison.
It was all sovereignly planned by God so that they could see something of the power of prayer. And they were in this prayer meeting.
And they saw the tremendous power of prayer how Peter God released.
And after that Barnabas and Saul went back to Jerusalem, taking along with them John who was called Mark and whose house this prayer meeting was going on.
And not only taking him back, but taking back with them the same spirit of prayer that they had been gripped by in Jerusalem.
And so we see in the next verse chapter 13 and verse 1 and 2. There were in Antioch in the church that was there prophets and teachers.
This is a very young church, newly coming up and yet in such a short time there were prophets and teachers in that church.
Barnabas, Simeon, Colniger, Lucius and Manine. There were at least four.
And Saul, including him five. Prophets and teachers.
And these five were praying. It says here in verse 2 they were ministering to the Lord and fasting.
Saul and Barnabas had no doubt come and told them the tremendous things they had seen in Jerusalem as a result of prayer.
And they decided to seek God themselves. And here they were not asking God for anything.
In the Old Testament fasting was always accompanied by prayer. People fasted and prayed usually and invariably asking God to do something for them.
But here is another type of fasting that we read in verse 2 which is fasting and worshipping.
Ministering means worshipping. Worshiping the Lord. Ministering to the Lord. Not ministering to the people, but ministering to the Lord.
They were fasting and worshipping. They were saying, Lord we don't want anything from you.
We're not fasting and praying asking you for anything. You've already done everything for us.
We're just fasting and worshipping you and praising you. And while they were in that atmosphere of praise, like it says in Psalm 22 verse 3, God dwells in the midst of the praises of his people.
God was there as they were fasting and worshipping. And while they were doing that the Holy Spirit said, set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.
It is in that atmosphere of praise that God speaks. God never speaks to a man who is full of complaints and grudges and grumbling etc.
But when a man is eliminated all that and has learned how to praise God and to worship him in that atmosphere, God speaks.
The Holy Spirit specifically said, set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.

Notice here that the Holy Spirit had already called Barnabas and Saul. In an earlier study we considered how New Testament prophecy does not direct people to do something without God having spoken to them directly.
We saw that when we consider the last verses of Acts 11. We see the same thing here. The Holy Spirit doesn't say, well now I'm telling you to set apart Barnabas and Saul. No.
No. Maybe the Holy Spirit spoke through a prophecy there. Or it was a witness that each person, each of those five felt in their spirit.
But it says here that the Holy Spirit said the work to which I have already called them.
In other words, the Holy Spirit had already spoken personally to Saul and Barnabas separately.
And God's calling for full-time work is always like that. It comes to us personally and individually first. And then it is confirmed by other godly men with whom we are associated.
It's extremely dangerous to step out into full-time Christian work without a specific call from God. God calls people to full-time Christian work even today like he did.
Peter and James and John from the seashores of Galilee like he called Paul. But it must be the result of a specific call personally to our own hearts first.
And then confirmed by the witness of other godly men who we are associated with. Then when they had fasted and prayed, laid their hands on them. They sent them away.
Then they laid hands on them and said, we are behind you. This is the right way. This is the scriptural way for people to go out into Christian ministry.

People go out on their own or people go out without a call. There are all types of problems. If we were to follow this scriptural pattern, we'd be saved from a lot of confusion in Christian work today.
Let's turn today to Acts of the Apostles chapter 13 and verse 3.
Here we read how after the Holy Spirit called Barnabason Saul for his ministry, individually he confirmed that call through Simeon, Lucius and Manain, their co-workers mentioned in verse 1.
This is God's pattern for Christian work, for Christian ministry. Those who are called to the ministry are first called personally, privately by the Holy Spirit.
And then that call is confirmed by others who are their co-workers, mature godly men. And then those other men, it says here, they fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them.
First of all, God spoke to them while they were fasting and worshipping him in verse 2. After God spoke, they again fasted and prayed and laid their hands on these two and sent them away.
And so being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Cilicia and from there they sailed to Cyprus.
I want you to notice here the importance that the early church gave to fasting and praying as we read in verse 2 and 3.
This is the first great missionary movement from the early church and it began in an atmosphere of prayer and fasting, worshipping and fasting.
And because Christians today have lost that understanding of seeking God together like that, they do not experience the Holy Spirit speaking to them.
Also, if we don't take our Christian life seriously, we cannot expect the Holy Spirit to speak to us.
The Holy Spirit spoke to them, these three laid hands on them and prayed for them and sent them out. They sent them away. Verse 3 we read in the last part.

These other three prophets and teachers. But verse 4 says they were sent out by the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit works through the members of Christ's body and they went down to Cilicia and from there they sailed to Cyprus.
And when they reached Salamis, they began to proclaim the Word of God in the synagogues of the Jews and they also had John as their helper.
Barnabas and Saul were ministering the Word and young John Mark was their helper.

And when they had gone through the whole island, as far as Pepos, they found a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet whose name was Bar Jesus, who was with the pro-cantal Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence.

This man summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the Word of God. But Alimas, the magician, for thus his name is translated, was opposing them, seeking to turn the pro-cantal away from the faith.
No doubt Alimas the magician was making a lot of money and having a lot of power being close to Sergius Paulus, the pro-cantal.

And so he tried to stop the pro-cantal from turning to the Lord.

No doubt by speaking against this doctrine, or speaking against Saul and Barnabas, but Saul, who was also known as Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, at that moment filled again with the Holy Spirit, fixed his gaze upon Alimas and said,
You who are full of all deceit and fraud, you son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, will you not cease to make crooked the straight ways of the Lord?
And now behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you and you will be blind, and not see the sun for a time, and immediately a mist and a darkness fell upon him.
And he went about seeking those who would lead him by the hand. Then the pro-cantal believed when he saw what had happened, being amazed at the teaching of the Lord.

What does he say? He turns round to this magician and says, You who are full of deceit and fraud, you son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, and so on.

And yet we saw in an earlier study in Acts chapter 8 how Peter spoke to another magician in Samaria.
In similar words, I see that you're in the gall of bitterness and the bondage of iniquity.
Here we find also Paul speaking even stronger words.
And just in case we're in any doubt as to whether Paul said that out of his own mind, we're told specifically that he was filled with the Holy Spirit at that moment.
Having just been filled with the Holy Spirit, he spoke under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit confirmed it by making Alimas blind.
But only for a season. That's the mercy of God. He wasn't permanently blind.
But look how he speaks to Alimas, you son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, will you not cease to make crooked the straight ways of the Lord?
There is a place for such rebuke when we're filled with the Holy Spirit to keep the church pure, to preach God's word.
There is a need in these days for men who have authority, men who know God, men who have waited in God's presence in fasting and prayer, sent out by the Holy Spirit, filled with the Holy Spirit.

And then people will believe, like it says the pro-consul believed.

God works in different ways at different times.

Jesus said, all authority in heaven and earth is given to me, therefore go and preach the gospel to every creature.
So that's what we see here. The authority of heaven and earth that Jesus has backs us up when we go out to preach the gospel and make disciples.
We read further in verse 13, now Paul and his companions put out the sea from Paphos and came to Perga and Pamphylia, and John left them and returned to Jerusalem.

And Paul stood up and motioning with his hand he said, here we read the strategy that Paul adopted in every single place he went to, generally speaking.

But if there was a synagogue, he went there and the best day to go to the synagogue was the Sabbath day when everybody was there.
And even though Paul had finished with the old covenant and finished with being a Jew and finished with the Sabbath and everything else,
he knew that there were most likely more God-fearing people in the synagogue than anywhere else.
